verses.text: While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper country, came to Ephesus, and found certain disciples.
He said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
He said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul said, “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus.”
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke with other languages and prophesied.
They were about twelve men in all.
He entered into the synagogue, and spoke boldly for a period of three months, reasoning and persuading about the things concerning God’s Kingdom.
But when some were hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he departed from them, and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.
God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul,
so that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out.
But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, took on themselves to invoke over those who had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.”
There were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who did this.
The evil spirit answered, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?”
The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overpowered them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived at Ephesus. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Many also of those who had believed came, confessing, and declaring their deeds.
Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.
Now after these things had ended, Paul determined in the spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”
Having sent into Macedonia two of those who served him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
About that time there arose no small stir concerning the Way.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen,
whom he gathered together, with the workmen of like occupation, and said, “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth.
You see and hear, that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods, that are made with hands.

Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.”
When they heard this they were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel.
When Paul wanted to enter in to the people, the disciples didn’t allow him.
Certain also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and begged him not to venture into the theater.
Some therefore cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was in confusion. Most of them didn’t know why they had come together.
They brought Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people.
But when they perceived that he was a Jew, all with one voice for a time of about two hours cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

When the town clerk had quieted the multitude, he said, “You men of Ephesus, what man is there who doesn’t know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis, and of the image which fell down from Zeus?
Seeing then that these things can’t be denied, you ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of your goddess.
If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a matter against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them press charges against one another.
But if you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in the regular assembly.
For indeed we are in danger of being accused concerning today’s riot, there being no cause. Concerning it, we wouldn’t be able to give an account of this commotion.”
When he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.

footnotes.content: Paul finds believers in Ephesus who'd heard John's message but nothing more. How like the Lord to meet us where we are, even when we're incomplete—then draw us deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's first question cuts to the heart: have you received the Spirit? Not the outward form, but the living breath of God. Sometimes we ask the simplest questions to learn the deepest truths.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John's baptism was real, but it pointed ahead. These faithful disciples had stopped at a signpost and built their house there, not seeing the one it pointed toward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul reminds them: John himself taught the way forward—believe on the One coming after. How gently Paul brings them home, not scolding their incompleteness but finishing the sentence John began.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They hear and turn, baptized into Jesus' name. A moment of joy—the confusion lifts, and they step into what they'd always been reaching for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul lays his hands on them and the Spirit falls—not as a reward for being clever, but as the Father's gift to the hungry and open. They speak in tongues and prophesy: the living God has come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve men. A small company, a remnant gathered. I think of how the Lord often works quietly among the few before the crowds wake up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For three months Paul speaks boldly in the synagogue at Ephesus, reasoning about God's Kingdom. His boldness came not from bluster but from time spent in prayer—he had counted the cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some hearts harden; some turn away and speak evil of the Way. Paul doesn't fight the hardness—he gathers those willing and moves to new ground, the school of Tyrannus. Wisdom knows when to leave a field fallow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For two years the gospel spreads across Asia through daily conversation. Not a crusade, but a steady, humble witness. The whole region hears—both those who come eager and those who come angry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God worked special miracles through Paul. Not tricks or show, but real power—the Kingdom breaking through, meeting real need. Power always points back to the One who gives it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even a cloth Paul touched carried healing. Such faith! The sick and demon-seized brought their desperation to the one through whom Christ moved, and received what they needed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some Jews, wandering exorcists, try to copy what Paul does—speaking Jesus' name like a magic password. They think power is a technique to master, not a gift to receive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven sons of Sceva, a chief priest. Men with authority and credentials, trying to do the apostle's work. Status and technique are not the same as the Spirit's authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The evil spirit speaks: 'Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?' The demon recognizes true servants of the Lord—there's a knowing in the unseen world that names who truly belongs to Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man possessed leaps on them with such violence they flee naked and wounded. A humbling, public failure—the exorcists' presumption stripped bare.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear falls on the city. All of Ephesus hears what happened, and the name of the Lord Jesus is magnified through this rebuke. Even the Lord's judgment speaks His greatness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many believers come confessing and declaring their deeds—the hidden things brought into light. Confession is where the Kingdom moves from secret to shared, from shame to belonging.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They burn their books of magic—fifty thousand pieces of silver worth of them, gone. Not out of compulsion but joy: they've found something far greater than power, and the old tools look empty now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The word of the Lord grows and becomes mighty. Not through the exorcists' tricks or the merchants' schemes, but through truth spoken, confession made, and lives turned toward Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul determines to go to Jerusalem, then Rome. He's drawn by the Spirit to the center of power, both religious and political. He doesn't yet know what waits for him—only that he's called forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Timothy and Erastus go ahead; Paul stays in Asia. Two men, sent as scouts—one would become Paul's closest friend. Faithfulness in the small errand leads to partnership in the great work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A stir about the Way rises in the city. Persecution is often quiet at first—just talk, just tension. Then it swells.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Demetrius, a silversmith who makes shrines to Artemis, sees his trade threatened. When the gospel touches a person's livelihood, suddenly he cares deeply about the goddess he once took for granted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He gathers the craftsmen: 'By this business we have our wealth.' The idol-makers speak plainly—their gods are their income. How often do we dress earthly concern in religious clothing?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Demetrius says Paul has turned many away from idols across Asia, saying they're not gods at all. One man, speaking Jesus, has unraveled what centuries of habit had bound tight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He warns that Artemis' temple and majesty will be 'counted as nothing.' Artemis has been worshipped by all Asia and the world—yet one name, Jesus, stands above her. The gospel shows what true greatness looks like.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men fill with anger and cry out: 'Great is Artemis!' But anger has replaced zeal—they're fighting to keep what they love rather than seeking what's true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Confusion sweeps the city; they rush to the theater and seize Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's traveling companions. The crowd, once gathered, becomes an instrument for whoever can shout loudest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul wants to go stand with his friends, but the disciples hold him back. Love says 'go stand with them,' but wisdom says 'let them stand for you now.' Both are true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some Asiarchs—officials of high rank—who are his friends beg Paul not to enter the theater. Even power respects the apostle; some hearts have turned toward truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The assembly cries out in confusion—some shouting one thing, some another. Most don't even know why they came. A mob is mostly fear and noise, not reason.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bring Alexander forward—the Jews presenting him to speak. Perhaps hoping he'll defend their innocence; perhaps sacrificing him to the crowd.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they see he's a Jew, they silence him with two hours of chanting 'Great is Artemis!' Prejudice is stronger than argument; the crowd has made its choice before hearing a word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The town clerk quiets the multitude and reminds them that Ephesus is the temple-keeper of Artemis and keeper of her image 'which fell down from Zeus.' Wisdom speaks plain fact—that famous image was a meteorite, held sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He says these things can't be denied, so 'be quiet and do nothing rash.' Quiet is the hardest counsel for an angry heart, but it's the beginning of wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul and his friends are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers—just men teaching. The clerk speaks truth to the crowd: they're about to condemn the innocent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If Demetrius has a legal grievance, the courts are open and proconsuls stand ready. Take it through proper channels, not through mob rage. Order holds more power than chaos.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Other matters can be settled in the regular assembly, in peace, with process. The clerk teaches: there's a way to do things that honors both truth and community.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He warns: 'We risk being accused of riot with no cause.' What guards the city's peace? Not weapons or walls, but officials who think and speak clearly when others are mad.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When he had spoken, he dismissed the assembly. Readers today hear an echo: how often does one voice speaking truth with calm authority scatter what a thousand angry voices have gathered? The Lord sends such people to their cities in every age.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
